blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The diversity of feeding structures in annelids can be classified into several functional categories. These feeding categories are not indicative of phylogenetic relationships but are useful for ecological purposes. A given functional category can contain taxa that have different buccal organs. The categories used here are derived from Fauchald and Jumars (1979) and Jumars et al. (2015).

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Many annelids eat mud or sand and may show little discrimination in the size or type of particles eaten. The sediment is ingested, and any digestible organic material is assimilated as it passes through the alimentary canal. This form of feeding is also called non-selective deposit feeding. Most groups using this method have a ventral simple proboscis or simple axial proboscis. Of the annelid groups that are non-selective deposit feeders, such as Arenicolidae (Fig. 2.10a) and Maldanidae, live in relatively permanent burrows or tubes and ingest the sediment in such a way that a continuous fall of sand or mud occurs in front of them to eat. Others, such as Orbinidae, do not have permanent burrows or tubes but move through the sediment, eating it as they tunnel. The amount of nutritional value in sediment varies but shallow-water mud deposits tend to carry the largest numbers of non-selective deposit feeders. The total organic matter in such areas can be as low 1–2% and most of the deposit feeders must eat continually. The processing time (from ingestion to passage through to the rectum) for the sediment can be as little as 15 minutes in taxa such as Arenicola marina (Kermack, 1955). As is discussed in some of the chapters dealing with specific taxa, it has been shown that several the so-called non-selective deposit feeders have sophisticated selective and sorting mechanisms.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Some deposit feeders do not ingest sediment haphazardly but use their palps or buccal organs to sort organic material from the sediment prior to ingestion. Others select sediment particles of a particular size range, usually the smaller particles. Smaller particles have a greater surface area to volume ratio than large particles, and so may be more proportionally covered with food. Many selective deposit feeders live in tubes, though the method of sorting varies according to the types of palps that are present. Terebelliformia can have their multiple palps, with the longitudinal ciliated grooves containing mucus, laid out over the sediment surface. The palps are extended by 'creeping' on cilia and detritus is selected or rejected. The selected particles stick to the mucus and are carried along the groove by ciliary action to the base of the palp. Each palp is wiped periodically on the lower lip where cilia carry the mucus plus detritus into the mouth. Annelids with only a single pair of grooved palps, such as Spionidae, use a similar method of feeding, sweeping the palps over the sediment surface or waving them in the water column to gather food. Other selective deposit feeders include Oweniidae (some) and possibly Opheliidae (Fauchald and Jumars, 1979; Jumars et al., 2015).

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: This term refers to annelids that use their proboscis, usually an eversible muscular ventral or muscular axial organ, to seize their food items. The two groups of annelids that have evolved jaws (Eunicida and Phyllodocida) use them to either seize live animals (carnivores), to tear off pieces of algae (herbivores), or to grasp dead and decaying matter (scavengers). Some of the raptorial groups such as the Phyllodocidae lack jaws and use their eversible proboscis to grasp prey.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Several annelid groups can collect particles suspended in the water column. All known filter-feeders live in some sort of tube or burrow. The best-known are Chaetopteridae, Sabellariidae, Sabellida, and Urechis (Thalassematidae). When the radiolar crown of Sabellida is expanded out of the tube a funnel is formed (Fig. 2.10j). The cilia beat and create a current in the surrounding water, which passes upwards through the crown into the funnel and swirls around the base of the funnel and then upwards and outwards. Food particles are trapped on the pinnules and carried into the groove by cilia. The ciliary current carries the particles towards the base of the crown where the material is sorted. Small particles are swallowed while large ones are pushed away from the mouth and drop into the water (Nicol, 1931). Some Sabellida sort the particles into three sizes, with mid-sized particles being used in the construction of the tube (Mayer, 1994). The suspension mechanisms of Chaetopteridae (Barnes, 1964; Barnes, 1965; MacGinitie, 1939) and Urechis have been well studied (Osovitz and Julian, 2002).

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Asexual reproduction in annelids is widespread and occurs in several different forms. It involves the subdivision of the body and regeneration of the missing parts and comes under a general term, schizotomy (Schroeder and Hermans, 1975). Schizotomy has been further divided by Schroeder and Hermans into two processes that are termed paratomy and archotomy. Paratomy refers to the formation of a recognizable complete individual that then separates from the 'parent' stock, whereas archotomy is simple fission or fragmentation of the body with no prior cephalization. There is, however, a grade between these two extremes. Paratomy occurs in annelid taxa such as Ctenodrilus (Pl. 13f) and some Spionidae (Fig. 42.4b) but is most well known in the Serpulidae and Sabellidae.
